stt: Ask HN: Best Mathematics book for complete noobie?
x:
I think Kreyszig's Advanced Engineering Mathematics is an excellent text in applied math.

I'm not sure where you're at or what direction you want to study, but once you're familiar with calculus concepts this text is a good place to go to deal with ODE and analysis.

stt: Ask HN: Are there books for mathematics like Feynman's lectures on physics?
x:
The Princeton Companions to Mathematics and Applied Mathematics are beautiful to leaf through at the library. They're also hardcore heavy-weight (physically) and unlikely to be read twice, so don't buy them.

My personal take is that good linear algebra books at any level are great "tours of mathematics". Start with Strang and never stop. In a few years you'll be balled up with Kreyszig scribbling proof attempts in receipts, flaming unkempt hair and everyone around you will think you're weird but you'll be so, so happy.

stt: Ask HN: The book that did it for you in math and/or CS?
x:
I will recommend books that I have and books that I heard of:

Books that sparked my interest in all of Mathematics (BTW, I'll be glad if you recommend any Abstract Algebra books):

- Calculus, Howard Anton.

- Calculus, Spivak

- Advanced Engineering Mathematics, Erwin Kreyszig

- Elementary Number Theory, David Burton.

Computer Science/Engineering:

- Data Structures and Algorithms, Adam Drozdek

- Digital Design, Morris Mano

- David Patterson and John Hennesey's  books

- Mastering Embedded Linux Programming, Chris Simmonds.
